title: Claude for Writers
author: Anthropic
summary: Anthropic's own use-case page showing how Claude fits into drafting, editorial feedback, and research phases of writing, with example prompts.
who_for: Anyone who wants Anthropic's own framing of what Claude is good for as a writing tool, before trying prompts themselves.
skip_if: You already use Claude daily for writing — this page is orientation, not a workflow.
notes: Official marketing page, not tutorial content; light on specifics like model choice or editing depth.

title: Claude for Marketing
author: Anthropic
summary: Anthropic's tutorial hub of short example workflows for marketing teams, including Cowork-based weekly reporting and Claude Design for decks.
who_for: Marketers wanting a menu of official example use cases to skim before picking one to try.
skip_if: You want copy-paste prompts or a step-by-step tutorial — this page mostly links out to short video examples.
notes: Page is a curated list of linked examples rather than a single how-to.

title: Understanding Claude's Personalization Features
author: Anthropic (Help Center)
summary: Official explanation of how profile preferences, project instructions, and styles differ, and when to use each for a consistent voice.
who_for: Anyone setting up Claude for a recurring writing role who is unsure where their voice rules should live.
skip_if: You've already got Projects and Styles configured — this is a conceptual explainer, not new tactics.
notes: Continuously updated help article (shown as 'Updated yesterday' at time of check); accurate as of Aug 2026.

title: How Can I Create and Manage Projects?
author: Anthropic (Help Center)
summary: Step-by-step official instructions for setting up a Claude Project with knowledge files and persistent instructions — the base setup for a consistent editorial voice.
who_for: Writers and editors who haven't yet set up a Project to hold style guides and reference material.
skip_if: You already run a Project with knowledge and instructions configured.
notes: Plan limits (e.g., how many projects on free vs. paid tiers) have shifted across versions of this article — check current limits in-app.

title: Organize Your Tasks With Projects in Claude Cowork
author: Anthropic (Help Center)
summary: Explains how Cowork projects combine instructions, scheduled tasks, local-folder context, and project-scoped memory for recurring document work.
who_for: Writers or editorial teams handling long-running, file-heavy projects (a book, a recurring report) who want Claude working directly on local files.
skip_if: You only do one-off chat-based writing tasks — Cowork setup overhead isn't worth it for that.
notes: Described as desktop-only with no cloud sync at time of writing — worth confirming current status in-app before relying on it for team handoffs.

title: Claude 101
author: Anthropic Academy
summary: Anthropic's official beginner course covering everyday Claude use and core features — 12 lectures, about an hour of video, no writing specialization.
who_for: Someone who has never used Claude and wants the vendor's own orientation before moving to writing-specific prompts.
skip_if: You've already completed onboarding or use Claude regularly — this is entry-level and not writing-specific.
notes: General-purpose, not tailored to writers; hosted on Anthropic's Skilljar platform and requires a free account login. | URL corrected 2026-08-19: claude.com/courses path was wrong, real course lives on Anthropic Academy (Skilljar).

title: Introduction to Claude Cowork
author: Anthropic Academy
summary: Short official course introducing the Cowork task loop, plugins, and skills for working on real files and projects.
who_for: Writers or editorial teams curious whether Cowork is worth setting up for document-heavy work.
skip_if: You do lightweight, single-document writing tasks in regular chat — Cowork's setup overhead likely won't pay off.
notes: Lecture count and video length weren't shown on the catalog page at time of check, so depth couldn't be confirmed. | URL corrected 2026-08-19: claude.com/courses path was wrong, real course lives on Anthropic Academy (Skilljar).

title: Multilingual Support
author: Anthropic (Platform Docs)
summary: Official documentation on how Claude handles languages beyond English, including guidance to account for cultural context rather than literal translation alone.
who_for: Translators and localization leads who want Anthropic's own account of language performance and prompting tips before building a workflow.
skip_if: You need production-grade localization tooling (glossaries, translation memory, QA) — this is prompting guidance, not a platform.
notes: Written primarily for an API/developer audience, but the prompting advice applies equally in the regular chat app.

title: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing
author: Wikipedia community (WikiProject AI Cleanup)
summary: A field guide, built from thousands of real cases, cataloguing the vocabulary, sentence patterns, and formatting habits that give away AI-generated text — the most thorough public resource on this topic.
who_for: Any writer or editor who wants a concrete, evidence-based checklist for catching and removing AI 'tells' before publishing.
skip_if: You want a short list — this runs to roughly 15,000 words and is written for Wikipedia editors first, general writers second.
notes: Descriptive, not prescriptive — the page itself warns that no single sign proves AI authorship; use it as a pattern-matching aid, not a detector.

title: The Ethics of Using AI
author: SPJ Ethics Central (Society of Professional Journalists)
summary: SPJ's early position statement on AI in journalism, prompted by the 2023 CNET AI-byline controversy, arguing AI use should be limited and judged case by case.
who_for: Anyone wanting the professional-body baseline position that predates most outlets' individual AI policies.
skip_if: You need current, specific rules — this predates SPJ's 2026 Code of Ethics revision (see next entry).
notes: Flagged as possibly outdated — more than 12 months old and written before most newsroom AI policies existed.

title: Proposed Revisions to SPJ's Code of Ethics (2026)
author: Society of Professional Journalists
summary: SPJ's first Code of Ethics revision since 2014, adding language on verifying AI-assisted work and holding journalists accountable regardless of what tool produced the content — deliberately avoids naming any AI product.
who_for: Journalists, editors, and freelancers who want current professional-body ethics language to cite or adapt for a newsroom policy.
skip_if: You need a ready-made newsroom operating policy — this is a professional code of conduct, not an operational AI policy document.
notes: Was under public member review at time of writing; exact language may still change before final adoption.

title: Creating a Public AI Policy for Your Newsroom
author: The Open Notebook
summary: A practical guide to what belongs in a newsroom's public AI policy, drawing on common threads across policies already published by other outlets.
who_for: An editor or small newsroom without an AI policy who needs a starting checklist of what to cover.
skip_if: You just want to read example policies rather than write one — go to individual outlet policies instead.
notes: Aimed at science/specialist journalism outlets, but the framework generalizes to most newsrooms.

title: The Guardian Updates Its AI Policies Around Training, Trust and In-House Tools
author: Journalism.co.uk
summary: Reports on The Guardian's March 2026 policy update, which now permits limited generative AI use (alt text, transcription, document analysis) with senior-editor approval and mandatory reader disclosure.
who_for: Anyone benchmarking their own disclosure policy against a major outlet that moved from an outright ban to a narrow, approved list of AI uses.
skip_if: You need the Guardian's full policy text verbatim — this is trade-press reporting on it, not the source document.
notes: Secondary reporting; a standalone public URL for the Guardian's own editorial code text was not independently located during this research.

title: How Three Newsrooms Are Charting Different Paths for AI Use
author: Erik P. Bucy and Milad Jalalian Ebrahimi, Nieman Journalism Lab
summary: A comparative case study of Reuters, the BBC, and The Guardian's AI policies, arguing each outlet's approach reflects its funding model and values rather than a shared industry standard.
who_for: Anyone wanting a comparative, researched view of how newsroom ownership models shape AI policy, not just one outlet's rules.
skip_if: You want operational how-to guidance rather than policy analysis.
notes: Written by academic media researchers and published via Nieman Lab and The Conversation; well-sourced against public policy documents and BBC/EBU research.

title: AP Sets New AI Standards for Newsroom Use
author: Romy Abu-Fadel, Media Copilot
summary: Short report on the Associated Press updating its AI standards to allow tools for headlines and summaries while keeping reporting and writing with journalists.
who_for: Anyone tracking how AP's position has shifted since its original 2023 guidelines.
skip_if: You need AP's full stylebook chapter on AI rather than a news summary of the update.
notes: Only a brief summary was available in search results; AP's own standards document was not independently located during this research.

title: How to Stop Claude Writing Like an AI
author: Will Francis
summary: A practical, copy-pasteable set of Custom Instructions and a banned-words list, built from Wikipedia's AI-writing-tells research plus the author's own year of producing content with Claude.
who_for: Anyone who wants a ready-to-use starting point for Custom Instructions rather than building a voice guide from scratch.
skip_if: You want a deep explanation of why each rule works — this is a practical toolkit, not a breakdown of the underlying research.
notes: Named individual author with a stated methodology (Wikipedia + GPTZero + Grammarly + personal use); reads as genuine practitioner writing, not content-farm output.

title: How to Spot AI Writing, According to Wikipedia
author: William Beutler, Beutler Ink
summary: A PR consultant's condensed, business-context version of Wikipedia's Signs of AI Writing guide, pulling out the seven patterns most recognizable outside an encyclopedia.
who_for: Someone who wants the Wikipedia guide's key points without reading the full ~15,000-word source.
skip_if: You've already read the full Wikipedia page — this doesn't add much beyond condensing it.
notes: Named author at an established PR/Wikipedia-strategy agency; explicitly credits Wikipedia as the source rather than presenting the analysis as original.

title: avoid-ai-writing (Claude Code / agent skill)
author: Conor Bronsdon
summary: An open-source skill that audits and rewrites text against a large, tiered word-replacement table and dozens of pattern categories, with a two-pass self-check before returning results.
who_for: Technical writers or teams already using Claude Code who want an automated, repeatable AI-tell check rather than a manual read-through.
skip_if: You don't use Claude Code or a similar agent tool — this doesn't work as a plain chat prompt.
notes: Only the README/description was reviewed, not the full source; the author's claims about detection-tier weighting were not independently verified.

title: Claude Skills for Journalism, Media & Academia
author: Joe Amditis (Center for Cooperative Media)
summary: A curated set of Claude Code skills for newsroom work — AP-style checks, AI-slop detoxing, source verification, FOIA requests, fact-checking, and editorial workflow — built by a journalism-innovation practitioner.
who_for: A newsroom or freelance journalist comfortable installing Claude Code who wants journalism-specific guardrails rather than generic writing skills.
skip_if: You only use the Claude.ai chat app — these skills require Claude Code.
notes: Author is affiliated with Montclair State University's Center for Cooperative Media, a real journalism-innovation body — one of the more credible practitioner sources found in this research.

title: Claude for Localization: Stop Starting Every Project from Zero
author: Dorota, Localize Like A Pro
summary: A localization consultant's argument for building a persistent context file (register, forbidden terms, client-specific rules) instead of re-explaining brief details in every new Claude conversation.
who_for: Freelance translators or localization managers using Claude ad hoc who are losing time re-establishing context each session.
skip_if: You already run Claude through Projects with saved context and glossaries — you're doing what this post recommends.
notes: Author runs paid training sessions on this exact topic, so the post is a soft pitch too — the free content itself is still specific and practical.

title: Claude, Editor
author: Restructured (Substack)
summary: A first-person account of using Claude as a developmental editor on a 7,000-word book proposal — checking clarity, cohesion, and flow, and reacting to late-night placeholder paragraphs.
who_for: Writers curious what working with Claude as an editor actually feels like in practice, told as a specific story rather than a generic feature list.
skip_if: You want a repeatable prompt or process — this is a narrative reflection, not a how-to.
notes: Author's identity/credentials weren't confirmed beyond the Substack byline; treat as one writer's anecdote, not an authoritative source.

title: Claude AI for Writing: The Complete Guide for Authors and Content Creators
author: Kenny Kane
summary: An author's account of using Claude across two of his own published books, covering manuscript structure and tone, and where Claude over-smooths voice unless explicitly told not to.
who_for: Book authors or long-form content creators who want a real practitioner's workflow rather than a generic feature tour.
skip_if: You want a neutral third-party review — Kane is a working author with his own books to promote, and this is personal experience, not independent testing.
notes: Named author with specific, checkable book titles referenced (The Accidental Nonprofiteer, Mission-Driven Ecommerce) — a genuine practitioner voice.

title: Set Your Standards Before You Start: A Journalist's Journey Using Claude.md
author: Stephen Stirling
summary: A 20-year journalist's account of building a personal CLAUDE.md with rules against fabricated quotes, mandatory verification flags, and AI-disclosure notes, with a sample file readers can adapt.
who_for: Individual journalists who want to set explicit ethical guardrails for their own Claude use rather than waiting for a newsroom-wide policy.
skip_if: You're not using Claude Code or a CLAUDE.md-style setup — the specific mechanism won't apply, though the underlying principles still would.
notes: Author discloses 20 years as a journalist and credits Joe Amditis (see the claude-skills-journalism entry) for guidance, which corroborates that source.

title: How I Use Claude Cowork to Write With AI in My Voice
author: Ran (ranthebuilder.cloud)
summary: A detailed walkthrough of a Cowork project setup — a CLAUDE.md file, an anti-AI style guide, and a custom LinkedIn-post-drafter skill — built by someone already using Claude heavily for coding.
who_for: Technically comfortable writers who want a concrete, file-by-file example of a voice-preserving Cowork setup to copy and adapt.
skip_if: You're not comfortable with folder structures and markdown config files — this assumes an engineering-adjacent comfort level.
notes: Author's primary audience is developers; the writing-voice content is a secondary application of a coding workflow, so parts may be more elaborate than a non-technical writer needs.

title: Claude AI Comprehensive Guide
author: Anton Voroniuk, SkillsBooster Academy (via Coursera)
summary: A six-module Coursera course with one module specifically on marketing and copywriting tasks (long-form content, landing pages, social media) using structured prompting.
who_for: Someone who wants a structured, assessed course path with a shareable certificate rather than piecing together blog posts.
skip_if: You don't want a Coursera Plus subscription — the course is listed as included with Coursera Plus rather than as a standalone free offering.
notes: Listed as 'Recently updated! February 2026'; only the syllabus was reviewed, not the video content, so the depth of the marketing module is unconfirmed.
